```{r setup}
# library(pitw)
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
.gg_pedantic(size = 0.5)
fig_dir = here::here("vignettes", "main", "fig")
set.seed(1001)
```

This vignette is the reference for **Figures 2 and 3** of the paper. It asks
the practical question that follows once the metrics have null distributions:
**how many predictions do you need before a test can see anything?**

Two simulations answer it from different directions.

| | Simulation 1 (Figure 2) | Simulation 2 (Figure 3) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | do the metrics separate known failures at realistic $n$? | how does each test's power build with $n$? |
| Design | $3\times3$ grid of dispersion calibration and bias | 4 named scenarios swept over $n$ |
| $n$ | 10, 100, 1000 | 10 log-spaced values from 10 to 1000 |
| Replicates | 100 per cell | 250 per point |
| Display | boxplots against critical values | median and 95% range against critical value |

Throughout, predictive distributions are normal and the dashed lines are the
analytical 5% critical values from `vignette("significance-testing")`,
evaluated at the relevant $n$. A metric above its dashed line is a rejection;
how far the *bulk* of the distribution sits above it is the power.

The paper describes both figures in more detail. The setup below is the
specification they refer back to.

# 1. Separation at fixed sample sizes (Figure 2)

The first simulation crosses the two failure modes that the adjustment is
meant to separate, at three sample sizes.

| Factor | Levels |
|---|---|
| dispersion calibration $\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E}$ | $2/3$ (overconfident), $1$ (calibrated), $3/2$ (conservative) |
| bias $\mu_\mathcal{E}$ | $0$ (unbiased), $0.5$ (medium), $1$ (high) |
| predictions per estimator $n$ | 10, 100, 1000 |
| replicate estimators | 100 per cell |

Two details matter for interpretation. The **error scale**
$\sigma_\mathcal{E}$ is itself redrawn log-uniformly on $[\tfrac12, 2]$ for
each replicate, with the claimed scale set to
$\sigma_\mathcal{S} = \sigma_\mathcal{E}\times$ calibration — so the
calibration *ratio* is held at its nominal level while the absolute scale
varies, and nothing can depend on the units. And
$\kappa_\mathcal{S} = 0$ throughout, so every prediction from a given
estimator claims the same width: spread–error decoupling is deliberately
excluded here and appears only in Simulation 2.

Bias is expressed in units of $\sigma_\mathcal{E}$, so "high" bias is a
one-standard-deviation displacement — large, but not absurd for a real
forecaster.

```{r}

# Simulation setup

bias_limit = 1
conf_range = 2
runs = 100
variability = 0 # this is a dispersion measure

config = tidyr::crossing(
  calibration = c(1/1.5, 1, 1.5),
  bias_location = c(0, 0.5, 1) * bias_limit,
  samples = c(10,100,1000),
  run = 1:runs
) %>% 
  dplyr::group_by(calibration, bias_location, samples) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    true_value = 0,
    bias_dist = "norm",
    bias_scale = exp(runif(runs, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_dist = "lnorm4",
    sharpness_location = bias_scale * calibration,
    sharpness_scale = variability
  )

sim = config %>% generate_simulation()
scores = sim %>% prediction_scores()

scores = scores %>% 
  mutate(
    confidence = case_when(
      calibration < 1 ~ "overconfident",
      calibration > 1 ~ "conservative",
      TRUE ~ "calibrated"
    ) %>%
      factor(levels = c("conservative", "calibrated", "overconfident")),
  bias = case_when(
      bias_location == 0.5 ~ "medium",
      bias_location == 1 ~ "high",
      TRUE ~ "unbiased"
    ) %>%
      factor(levels = c( "unbiased", "medium", "high")),
  samples = as.factor(samples)
  )

```


```{r}

crit_b = pitw::b_pit_significance(NA, c(10,100,1000))

plot1a = ggplot(scores, aes(y=B_pit, x = confidence, colour= bias, fill = bias))+
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE, alpha = 0.2)+
  geom_hline(data = crit_b, aes(yintercept = critical_0.05), linetype="dashed")+
  facet_wrap(~ n_predictions)+
  ylab("Baseline pit-w")+
  xlab(NULL)

crit_d = pitw::d_pit_significance(NA, c(10,100,1000))

plot1b = ggplot(scores, aes(y=D_pit, x = confidence, colour= bias, fill = bias))+
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE, alpha = 0.2)+
  geom_hline(data = crit_d, aes(yintercept = critical_0.05), linetype="dashed")+
  geom_hline(data = crit_d, aes(yintercept = -critical_0.05), linetype="dashed")+
  facet_wrap(~ n_predictions)+
  ylab("Directed pit-w")+
  xlab(NULL)

crit_u = pitw::u_pit_significance(NA, c(10,100,1000))

plot1c = ggplot(scores, aes(y=U_pit, x = confidence, colour= bias, fill = bias))+
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE, alpha = 0.2)+
  geom_hline(data = crit_u, aes(yintercept = critical_0.05), linetype="dashed")+
  facet_wrap(~ n_predictions)+
  ylab("Undirected pit-w")+
  xlab(NULL)


plot1 = plot1a+plot1b+plot1c+patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")+patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect",axes="collect_x", ncol=1)

.gg_save_as(
  plot1,
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig2-critical-limits"),
  size = std_size$two_third,
  formats = c("pdf", "eps")
)
```


Reading Figure 2, panel by panel. Each panel is one sample size; within it,
boxes are grouped by true dispersion calibration and coloured by bias.

**Panel A, $B_{pit}$.** The baseline metric responds to both failures at once.
Boxes rise with bias (colour) *and* away from the calibrated centre group, so
a rejection is informative only in the weakest sense: something is wrong. At
$n = 10$ the critical value is high enough that only the grossest failures
clear it; by $n = 1000$ almost everything does, including combinations that
are only mildly miscalibrated.

**Panel B, $D_{pit}$.** Two dashed lines, because the directed test is signed
and two-sided. The colour groups now sit **on top of one another**: bias moves
the boxes hardly at all, which is the bias invariance of Figure 1 shown as a
distribution rather than a scatter. What separates the boxes is dispersion
calibration, and it separates them by *sign* — conservative below zero,
overconfident above.

**Panel C, $U_{pit}$.** The undirected adjusted metric is also flat in colour,
and like $B_{pit}$ it is a distance so only the upper critical value applies.
It separates calibrated from miscalibrated but, unlike panel B, cannot say
which direction.

The practical message is in the leftmost panel: at $n = 10$ the boxes for
different calibration levels overlap heavily and sit largely below their
critical values. **Ten predictions is not enough to diagnose anything but a
gross failure.** By $n = 100$ the groups are cleanly separated, which is the
sample size the paper recommends as a working minimum.

For comparison, the two conventional summaries over the same simulation:

```{r}
ggplot(scores, aes(y=mean_coverage.0.5, x = confidence, colour= samples, fill = samples))+
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE, alpha = 0.2)+
  facet_wrap(~ bias)+
  ylab("mean 50% coverage")

```
```{r}
ggplot(scores, aes(y=mean_crps, x = confidence, colour= samples, fill = samples))+
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE, alpha = 0.2)+
  facet_wrap(~ bias)+
  ylab("mean CRPS")

```
Coverage is ordered correctly by dispersion calibration but is insensitive to
sample size in its central tendency — more data narrows the boxes without
moving them — and has no reference line to test against. Mean CRPS is ordered
mainly by bias, as in Figure 1 panel A. Neither supports a decision rule.

# 2. Power against sample size (Figure 3)

The second simulation replaces the grid with four **named scenarios**, each a
single well-defined failure mode, and sweeps the number of predictions
continuously. This is the figure to use when choosing $n$.

| Scenario | $\mu_\mathcal{E}$ | $\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E}$ | $\kappa_\mathcal{S}$ | Should be detected by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| unbiased; calibrated | 0 | 1 | 0 | nothing — this is the null |
| biased; calibrated | 1 | 1 | 0 | $B_{pit}$ only |
| unbiased; overconfident | 0 | $2/3$ | 0 | $D_{pit}$ and $U_{pit}$ |
| unbiased; calibrated; decoupled | 0 | 1 | 1 | $U_{pit}$, weakly $B_{pit}$ |

Here the error scale is **fixed** at $\sigma_\mathcal{E} = 1$ rather than
redrawn, so the only thing varying along each curve is $n$. Sample sizes are
the 10 log-spaced values from 10 to 1000, with 250 replicate estimators at
each; the lines are medians and the ribbons the central 95% of replicates.

The critical-value curves are evaluated on a finer grid of 100 sample sizes so
that they render as smooth $1/\sqrt{n}$ decays rather than as segments.

```{r}

# Second simulation setup
# N.B. overwrites config and scores from above

bias_limit = 1
conf_range = 2
runs = 250
variability = 0 # this is a dispersion measure

config = tidyr::crossing(
  samples = floor(10^seq(1,3,length.out=10)),
  run = 1:runs,
  tidyr::nesting(
    panel = forcats::as_factor(c("unbiased; calibrated", "biased; calibrated","unbiased; overconfident", "unbiased; calibrated; decoupled")),
    bias_location = c(0,1,0, 0),
    calibration = c(1, 1, 2/3, 1),
    sharpness_scale = c(0,0,0,1),
  )
) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(
    true_value = 0,
    bias_dist = "norm",
    bias_scale = 1, #exp(runif(runs, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_dist = "lnorm4",
    sharpness_location = bias_scale * calibration,
    `(σₑ/σₛ)` = forcats::as_factor(sprintf("%0.2f",calibration))
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(calibration, `(σₑ/σₛ)`, panel, samples)

sim = config %>% generate_simulation()
scores = sim %>% prediction_scores()

crit_b = pitw::b_pit_significance(NA,floor(10^seq(1,3,length.out=100)))
crit_d = pitw::d_pit_significance(NA,floor(10^seq(1,3,length.out=100)))
crit_u = pitw::u_pit_significance(NA,floor(10^seq(1,3,length.out=100)))

```


```{r}

plot_b = scores %>% ungroup() %>% group_by(samples, calibration, `(σₑ/σₛ)`, panel) %>% summarise(
  q.0.05 = quantile(B_pit, 0.025),
  q.0.5 = median(B_pit),
  q.0.95 = quantile(B_pit, 0.975)
)

plot2a = ggplot(plot_b, aes(y=q.0.5,ymin=q.0.05,ymax=q.0.95, x = samples))+
  geom_line(mapping=aes(colour=panel))+
  geom_line(data=crit_b, mapping=aes(x=n_predictions, y=critical_0.05), linetype="dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE)+
  geom_ribbon(mapping=aes(fill=panel),alpha=0.2)+
  scale_x_log10(n.breaks=9)+
  ylab("Baseline pit-w")+
  .gg_narrow(45)

plot_d = scores %>% ungroup() %>% group_by(samples, calibration, `(σₑ/σₛ)`, panel) %>% summarise(
  q.0.025 = quantile(D_pit, 0.025),
  q.0.5 = median(D_pit),
  q.0.975 = quantile(D_pit, 0.975)
)

plot2b = ggplot(plot_d, aes(y=q.0.5,ymin=q.0.025,ymax=q.0.975, x = samples))+
  geom_line(mapping=aes(colour=panel))+
  geom_line(data=crit_d, mapping=aes(x=n_predictions, y=critical_0.05), linetype="dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE)+
  geom_line(data=crit_d, mapping=aes(x=n_predictions, y=-critical_0.05), linetype="dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE)+
  geom_ribbon(mapping=aes(fill=panel),alpha=0.2)+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0)+
  scale_x_log10(n.breaks=9)+
  ylab("Directed pit-w")+
  .gg_narrow(45)

plot_u = scores %>% ungroup() %>% group_by(samples, calibration, `(σₑ/σₛ)`, panel) %>% summarise(
  q.0.05 = quantile(U_pit, 0.025),
  q.0.5 = median(U_pit),
  q.0.95 = quantile(U_pit, 0.975)
)

plot2c = ggplot(plot_u, aes(y=q.0.5,ymin=q.0.05,ymax=q.0.95, x = samples))+
  geom_line(mapping=aes(colour=panel))+
  geom_line(data=crit_u, mapping=aes(x=n_predictions, y=critical_0.05), linetype="dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE)+
  geom_ribbon(mapping=aes(fill=panel),alpha=0.2)+
  scale_x_log10(n.breaks=9)+
  ylab("Undirected pit-w")+
  .gg_narrow(45)

plot2 = plot2a+plot2b+plot2c+patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")+patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect",axes="collect_x", ncol=3)&theme(legend.position = "bottom")

.gg_save_as(
  plot2,
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig3-three-part-test"),
  size = std_size$third,
  formats = c("pdf", "eps")
)
```

Reading Figure 3. In each panel the dashed line falls as $1/\sqrt{n}$ — the
test gets more sensitive with more data — while a curve that stays above it is
a failure the test detects, and one that tracks below it is a failure that
test is blind to.

**Panel A, $B_{pit}$.** The null scenario tracks the critical value, as it must.
The biased scenario sits far above it at every $n$: a one-$\sigma$ bias is
detected from the smallest samples. The overconfident scenario also separates,
but later. The decoupled scenario rises above the line only slowly — the
omnibus test is the *weakest* of the three against spread–error decoupling.

**Panel B, $D_{pit}$.** The biased curve now sits on zero, inside the two
critical lines, at every sample size: the directed metric does not see a pure
location error, by construction. Only the overconfident scenario leaves the
band, and it does so with a definite sign. Note also that the decoupled
scenario stays within the band — $D_{pit}$ is insensitive to $\kappa$ as well
as to bias, which is what makes it a clean test of median width.

**Panel C, $U_{pit}$.** The biased curve again sits on the null, confirming
bias invariance. Both genuine miscalibrations — overconfidence and decoupling —
separate, and the decoupled scenario separates *earlier here than in panel A*.
Paying for the tighter adjusted null buys power against shape failures.

Taken together the three panels are the three-part test working as intended:
the pattern of which curves clear which lines identifies the failure mode,
rather than merely flagging that one exists. The crossing points also give the
direct answer to the sample-size question — read off where the scenario of
interest leaves the dashed line.

Two caveats carried over from `vignette("significance-testing")`: the
$D_{pit}$ critical value is mildly anti-conservative below $n \approx 50$, so
the left-hand end of panel B is optimistic; and all of this assumes
independent predictions.
